claims.text: Single-crystal FeNiCrMn exhibits anomalously weak yield-strength sensitivity to strain rate during the elastic-to-plastic transition.
The onset of yielding is dominated by thermally activated collective cross-slip of super-dislocations on {111} planes.
Dislocation nucleation from defects is not the dominant mechanism for the onset of yielding.
An FCC-to-BCC phase transformation is not the dominant deformation mechanism.
High lattice-friction stress and local chemical ordering are inherent to equiatomic FeNiCrMn and cause the proposed cross-slip behavior.
The initial single-crystal alloy is solutionized and FCC.
The initial material is free of pre-existing dislocation loops.
Local chemical short-range-order clusters and high Peierls barriers facilitate formation of sessile super-dislocations.
The proposed super-dislocations require thermally activated cross-slip to bypass local chemical obstacles.
At low temperatures, high Peierls stress prevents easy dislocation glide.
Increasing temperature supplies the activation energy required for cross-slip.
Yield stress is temperature dependent but largely strain-rate independent because thermal barrier crossing, rather than dislocation velocity, is rate limiting.
In traditional metals, dislocation multiplication and velocity dominate strain-rate sensitivity.
Yield strength will decrease strongly with increasing temperature.
Yield stress will remain approximately constant across three to four orders of magnitude in strain rate.
In-situ diffraction will show no BCC phase peaks during yielding.
Acoustic-emission signals will correlate with discrete cross-slip events rather than continuous nucleation bursts.
Pure Ni and Cu typically show increasing yield strength with increasing strain rate and decreasing yield strength with increasing temperature.
The hypothesis applies only to low-defect-density single crystals.
Polycrystals or samples with high initial dislocation densities may have different strain-rate sensitivities because of grain-boundary or forest-dislocation interactions.

contradictions.description: The proposed strain-rate interval of 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1 spans six orders of magnitude, whereas the predicted outcome describes constancy across only three to four orders.

The mechanism identifies thermally activated barrier crossing as the rate-limiting step but simultaneously uses that characterization to argue for negligible strain-rate dependence. Without an additional saturation or timescale argument, a rate-limiting activated process would ordinarily imply dependence on the available loading time.

The initial state is described as free of pre-existing dislocation loops and the hypothesis rejects dislocation nucleation as dominant, yet yielding is attributed to cross-slip of existing super-dislocations without specifying how the required mobile dislocations are initially supplied.
